The Hezbollah Tunnels: What Does This Underground City Look Like?

🔠🅰️🔠🔠1️⃣

The Hezbollah tunnel that runs under the small hilltop town of Majdal Zoun in southern Lebanon bears little resemblance to the crude, hand-dug passages of the Gaza underground.

About 170m long, and 20m beneath the shattered Shia village, the spacious and hardened facility is said to have benefited from Iranian design and engineering.

When The Telegraph was guided in by Israel Defense Forces (IDF) troops with night vision goggles in the early hours of Friday, it felt like a municipal underpass from the 1970s.

“A village the size of Majdal Zoun would have no need for such a large underground structure,” noted Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council. “[It’s] definitely Hezbollah.”

The concrete passage was littered with the detritus of war. Heavy blast doors gave way to several anterooms for weapons storage.

Branching tunnels were said by the IDF to have offered commanding views of Israel and been used to launch munitions until they were bombed.

“It’s a terror stronghold,” said a commander of Israel’s 551st Brigade, gesturing towards a room in which eight tons of explosives were said to have been found.

The floor was lined with the components of dozens of drones. “These one-way unmanned aerial vehicles are GPS guided and have a range of more than 200km [124 miles],” he said.

It is upon the fate of dozens of villages like Majdal Zoun – which sits, shattered and broken, on high ground just three miles north of the Israeli border – that the US-Iran ceasefire will be made or broken.

JD Vance, the US vice-president, was in Switzerland on Sunday, saying the flashpoint area was high on the agenda of the US-Iran talks that were taking place there.

Meanwhile, the IDF appeared to be preparing for an assault on a second village with an extensive tunnel network some 22 miles to the north-east of Majdal Zoun.

“I think we’re going to hopefully make progress on the nuclear issue, make progress on the Lebanon ceasefire issue. Those are the two big things that I think we’re to be focused on,” Mr Vance told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews.

Southern Lebanon’s towns – and the Hezbollah infrastructure some of them conceal – threaten to upend the wider US-Iran ceasefire.

Israel wants to hold them, to create a buffer zone that protects its northern communities. It fears that if it allows Lebanon’s Shia population to return, Hezbollah will come too, to dig in once more and rearm.

The Lebanese, on the other hand, see Israel as the aggressor – one that has destabilised the region for decades by failing to settle the Palestinian question.

The latest incursion, which began in response to Hezbollah rocket fire at the start of the Iran war, has taken some 6 per cent of Lebanese territory.

It has displaced more than a million people and strengthened Hezbollah’s populist resistance narrative, observers say.

“When Hezbollah launched their first rocket barrage on March 2, the feedback from the Shia community writ large was: ‘Oh my god, what have you done? We’re only just recovering from the previous round. Now you’re dragging us into another war,’” said Mr Blanford.
